rules.sentence: If there is AIN neuropraxia, the patient will be unable to flex the interphalangeal joint of the thumb and the distal interphalangeal joint of the index finger (cannot make an "OK" sign).
AIN palsy is found in 7.6% to 8.6% of supracondylar fractures and by itself, makes up 47% of all nerve-related complications and 70% of median nerve injuries.

Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome presents as a rare motor neuropathy involving the flexor pollicis longus, the radial portion of the flexor digitorum profundus, and the pronator quadratus, without associated sensory loss.
Clinicians must distinguish true anterior interosseous nerve syndrome—often attributed to idiopathic immune-mediated neuritis—from isolated traumatic nerve injuries and local tendon pathologies.

Conservative management remains the initial approach; surgical exploration and decompression may follow after failed nonoperative treatment, particularly in cases involving identifiable compressive lesions.
Nearly all cases of neuropraxia following supracondylar humerus fractures resolve spontaneously.
This course reviews anterior interosseous nerve anatomy and the syndrome's clinical presentation, diagnostic strategies, and differential diagnoses.
